patterns: why can i not get the weather
entries.answer: Weather is the state of the atmosphere at a place over hours or days, and I can explain the system that produces it, but I cannot tell you what it is doing in your town right now. There is no live source behind me, and a made-up temperature is worse than no answer. What I can do is describe how weather works, why forecasts are uncertain, and how to read one properly.

patterns: how far ahead is a forecast accurate
entries.answer: A forecast is a statement about what the weather will probably do, and the word probably is doing more work than most people notice. It is produced by simulating the atmosphere with current observations fed in, so the further ahead it goes the more it depends on assumptions that can fail. Skill varies sharply with lead time and with geography: a sea breeze is predictable, a convective storm three hours out is close to a coin toss, which is why forecasts are given as ranges.

patterns: is climate change the same as weather
entries.answer: Climate is the weather averaged over decades, which is the whole difference and the reason the two words are used loosely. A cold week is not climate change, and a warm decade is not weather. The metrics are averages and extremes, and both matter, since a heatwave that becomes routine is the more serious signal even though the average has barely moved. This is also why climate is discussed in tens of years while weather is discussed in hours.

entries.answer: A storm is a system of organised wind and rain produced by air rising, and storms are named by type depending on what sustains them. Tropical cyclones need warm ocean water and rotate because of the planet's spin, which is why they do not form near the equator. Thunderstorms are convection on a small scale, and the danger in them is lightning rather than wind, which is why the advice is to get indoors rather than to shelter from the rain.

patterns: why does humidity make heat feel worse
entries.answer: Humidity is the amount of water vapour in air, and the number people quote is usually relative humidity, which is the amount as a percentage of what the air could hold at that temperature. That makes the figure hard to read on its own: 60 per cent feels very different at 15 degrees and at 35. The thing that actually affects people is how quickly sweat evaporates, which is why humid heat feels worse than dry heat at the same temperature.
